damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Portkey walk/arrival at campsite
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Arthur as the knowledgeable, enthusiastic guide who explains Portkeys in detail to Harry and Hermione, describing how they work, why they use them, and the logistics of getting 100,000 wizards to the Cup without Muggle detection. He is eager, informed, and genuinely enjoys sharing the wizarding world's complexity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Arthur says 'Haven't the foggiest. Keep up!' when Ron asks where they're going, and provides almost no explanation of Portkeys or the logistical wizarding world detail. His role as informed, enthusiastic explainer is reduced to cheerful crowd-wrangling ('Keep up, girls!', 'Home sweet home.', 'Excellent, excellent.').
damaging_scenes.explanation: Arthur's delight in explaining the wizarding world to Muggle-raised Harry is a core character trait. The 'Haven't the foggiest' line directly contradicts the book Arthur, who absolutely knows where they're going and is keen to explain it all. It reduces him from an enthusiastic, knowledgeable Ministry man to a bumbling father figure, altering how the audience understands his character.

damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Arthur's comedy around Muggle artifacts and practices as warm, specific, and rooted in genuine fascination. He gets overexcited using the mallet to pitch the tent, struggles to light matches while having 'the time of his life,' and his enthusiasm is portrayed as endearing obsession. He also enforces anti-Muggle security rules with clear reasoning.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film skips the entire match-lighting scene and Arthur's gleeful incompetence with Muggle tools. His Muggle enthusiasm is reduced to a brief 'I love magic' moment from Harry and Arthur moving in the background. The anti-Muggle security lecture ('When real Muggles camp, they cook on fires outdoors. I've seen them at it!') is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The match-lighting scene is one of Arthur's most defining comic characterization moments in the books — his joy is specific, warm, and humanizing. Its absence removes a key window into his personality. The Muggle-obsession trait, while hinted at in the film, loses its best illustrative moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Ludo Bagman bet / twins gambling
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Arthur placing a modest one-Galleon bet himself, then actively trying to dissuade Fred and George from betting all their savings, expressing genuine parental concern ('Boys, I don't want you betting.... That's all your savings... Your mother—'). He watches on 'helplessly' as Bagman overrides him, showing a man who has moral authority but is outgunned socially.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The entire Bagman campfire scene — including the bet, Arthur's concern for the twins' savings, the discussion about Bertha Jorkins, and Arthur's nuanced relationship with Bagman and Crouch — is completely absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene establishes Arthur as a father who genuinely tries to protect his children financially, even when socially outmaneuvered. It also shows his collegial relationships at the Ministry and his quiet concern about Bertha Jorkins. Its absence flattens his characterization at the Cup.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Top Box / Malfoy confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Arthur responding to Lucius Malfoy's sneering insult about selling his house for tickets with a 'very strained smile' — he is humiliated but dignified, holding his composure in front of his children and the Minister of Magic. The dynamic illustrates the class and status tension that defines Arthur's position in wizarding society.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes Lucius's 'if it rains, you'll be the first to know' taunt directed at the Weasleys in the stands, but Arthur has no visible response or moment of strained dignity. The confrontation is entirely between Lucius and the children, with Arthur absent from the exchange.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Arthur's strained but dignified response to Malfoy's cruelty is a small but important character moment — it shows he bears the weight of the family's poverty with quiet pride. His absence from the film's version of this exchange removes that dimension and transfers the dynamic entirely to the younger generation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Death Eater attack at the campsite
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Arthur rolling up his sleeves, taking charge with calm authority, directing each child specifically ('You lot — get into the woods, and stick together. I'll come and fetch you when we've sorted this out!'), and then actively participating in the Ministry response to the Death Eater attack. He is effective, purposeful, and clearly a capable adult wizard under pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Arthur briefly saying 'Get back to the Portkey, everybody, and stick together! Fred, George! Ginny is your responsibility. Go!' before leaving. He then reappears only to run toward the Stupefy scene shouting 'Stop! That's my son!' His active Ministry role in fighting Death Eaters is not depicted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While the film does show Arthur directing the children and rushing to Ron's defense, his active role as a Ministry responder combating Death Eaters is invisible. The book's Arthur is a participant in the crisis response; the film's Arthur is primarily a worried father. This is a modest but real reduction in his agency and competence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Post-Dark Mark confrontation with Barty Crouch Sr.
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Arthur playing an active, reasoned role in the investigation: he defends Harry and the children ('Amos, think who you're talking to! Is Harry Potter likely to conjure the Dark Mark?'), provides logical analysis of how Winky could have found the wand innocently, challenges Diggory's rush to judgment, and speaks up kindly to Winky even as Crouch dismisses her. He is the voice of reason and fairness throughout the scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Arthur's contributions in this scene are reduced to 'Crouch, you can't possi--', 'Barty! They're just kids.', 'A man, Harry? Who?' and nodding. The detailed defense of Harry, the logical reconstruction of Winky's innocence, and his advocacy for fair treatment of the house-elf are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Arthur's strongest scenes in Goblet of Fire — he demonstrates moral clarity, logical reasoning, and fairness under pressure from a senior Ministry official. The film reduces him to a bystander who barely protests. His key function as the voice of reason and fairness is lost, which damages the audience's understanding of his character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Arthur's speech about the Dark Mark's terror
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains Arthur's deeply felt explanation to Ron of what the Dark Mark meant during Voldemort's reign: 'Ron, You-Know-Who and his followers sent the Dark Mark into the air whenever they killed... Just picture coming home and finding the Dark Mark hovering over your house, and knowing what you're about to find inside... Everyone's worst fear... the very worst...' Arthur winces as he speaks. This is one of his most emotionally significant moments — conveying the generational trauma of Voldemort's first reign.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This explanation is entirely absent from the film. The Dark Mark's significance is explained briefly by Hermione on the Hogwarts Express ('It's the Dark Mark, Harry. It's his mark') with no emotional weight from Arthur's lived experience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Arthur's Dark Mark speech is one of his most emotionally resonant moments in the entire saga — it conveys that he lived through genuine terror and that this isn't abstract history. Its removal loses the intergenerational trauma dimension of his character and weakens the film's establishment of how fearful the wizarding world is of Voldemort's return.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – Arthur at the maze finale / Cedric's death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not feature Arthur at the maze finale in the same way, but the film corpus is the relevant baseline here. The book establishes Arthur throughout as a man who takes the welfare of others seriously and acts with moral seriousness in moments of crisis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Arthur's response to Cedric's death is to hug Amos and giggle with him ('Arthur and Amos: Aha! Arthur: He did it!') — this appears to be timed to the moment Harry and Cedric arrive back, before the horror is apparent. While contextually the cheer may precede the realization, Arthur is then shown hugging Amos and giggling as Fleur screams, which creates a jarring tone mismatch for a character the books establish as emotionally serious and empathetic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'giggling' with Amos in the immediate vicinity of Cedric's death scene is a tonal inconsistency with the Arthur established in the books as deeply empathetic and emotionally responsive. It is brief but incongruous given the scene's gravity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Dursley fireplace / pickup scene entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book opens Arthur's GoF material with an extended, rich scene at the Dursleys: Arthur blasting through the blocked fireplace, his genuine fascination with the electric fire and plugs ('Eclectic, you say? With a plug?'), his awkward attempts at conversation with the Dursleys, his moral intervention forcing Vernon to say goodbye to Harry ('You aren't going to see your nephew till next summer... Surely you're going to say good-bye?'), and his angry but principled response to Fred's toffee prank on Dudley. This scene establishes Arthur's warmth, humor, moral backbone, Muggle obsession, and his relationship with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The entire Dursley pickup scene is absent from the film. The film begins with the group already leaving the Burrow for the World Cup.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single largest loss of Arthur characterization in the film. The Dursley pickup scene is his richest early-film opportunity: it establishes his Muggle fascination concretely, his moral courage (standing up to Vernon over Harry's dignity), his warm relationship with Harry as a surrogate father figure, and the Fred/George toffee argument which shows his principled stance on wizard-Muggle relations. Its complete removal is the most structurally damaging omission for the character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Absence of Arthur's post-World Cup Ministry work and Daily Prophet scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Arthur returning exhausted from Ministry cleanup work after the World Cup attack, reading the Daily Prophet coverage with frustration ('Ministry blunders... culprits not apprehended'), worrying about being quoted as a Ministry official, and ultimately feeling he made things worse. Mrs. Weasley's clock showing his hand at 'work' for weeks conveys the human cost. He is shown as a conscientious, hardworking civil servant carrying the weight of institutional failure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: All of this post-Cup Ministry fallout material is absent from the film. Arthur does not appear between the World Cup and the Hogwarts term beginning.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This material humanizes Arthur beyond 'enthusiastic dad' — he is a man who takes his professional responsibilities seriously, feels the weight of institutional failure, and works himself to exhaustion out of duty. Its absence removes important texture from his characterization as a Ministry employee with moral investment in his work.

main_damage_causes: Complete omission of the Dursley fireplace pickup scene, which is Arthur's single richest characterization moment in Goblet of Fire, establishing his Muggle obsession concretely, his moral courage with Vernon, his surrogate-father relationship with Harry, and his principled stance on wizard-Muggle relations.

Reduction of Arthur's agency and reasoning in the post-Dark Mark confrontation scene, removing his role as the calm, logical voice of fairness who defends Harry and advocates for Winky, replacing it with near-silent bystander status.

Absence of Arthur's emotionally resonant Dark Mark speech to Ron, which is his primary vehicle for conveying generational trauma and establishing the human stakes of Voldemort's return — this loss weakens both his character depth and the film's thematic grounding.
